what_its_for: Loratadine is an antihistamine used to relieve allergy symptoms such as runny nose, sneezing, itchy or watery eyes, and itching of the nose or throat. It is also used to treat hives (itchy skin rash). It works by blocking histamine, a natural substance your body makes during an allergic reaction.
how_to_take: Take loratadine exactly as directed on the package or as your doctor tells you. Swallow tablets whole with a full glass of water. If using dissolving tablets (RediTabs), place the tablet on your tongue and let it melt — you do not need water. If using liquid (syrup), use the measuring cup or spoon that comes with the package — do not use a regular kitchen spoon. You can take loratadine with or without food.
dosing: Adults and children 6 years and older: Take 10 mg (one tablet, one dissolving tablet, or 2 teaspoons of syrup) once a day. Do not take more than one dose in 24 hours. Children 2 to 5 years old: The usual dose is 5 mg (1 teaspoon of syrup or one 5 mg chewable tablet) once a day. Always check the package label for the correct dose for children.
missed_dose: If you miss a dose, take it as soon as you remember. However, if it is almost time for your next dose, skip the missed dose and continue with your regular schedule. Do not take two doses at the same time to make up for a missed one.
storage: Store loratadine at room temperature, between 68°F and 77°F (20°C to 25°C). Keep it away from heat, moisture, and direct sunlight. Do not store it in the bathroom. Keep all medications out of reach of children and pets. Dispose of unused or expired medication safely — ask your pharmacist about a medication take-back program.
what_to_avoid: Avoid taking more than the recommended dose. Although loratadine is less likely to cause drowsiness than older antihistamines, some people may still feel sleepy — use caution when driving or operating heavy machinery until you know how this medicine affects you. Avoid drinking alcohol while taking loratadine, as it may increase drowsiness. Tell your doctor or pharmacist about all other medicines you are taking, including over-the-counter drugs and supplements, to avoid interactions.
when_to_call_doctor: Contact your doctor or seek medical attention right away if you experience: a severe allergic reaction (rash, swelling of the face, lips, tongue, or throat, difficulty breathing or swallowing), fast or irregular heartbeat, severe dizziness, or if your symptoms do not improve after 3 days of use. Also call your doctor if you have liver or kidney disease before taking this medication, as a lower dose may be needed.
when_it_works: Loratadine usually starts working within 1 to 3 hours after taking a dose. You should notice relief from your allergy symptoms within the first day. It provides 24 hours of continuous symptom relief with just one daily dose.
special_populations: Older adults (65+): Loratadine is generally considered safe for older adults and is preferred over older antihistamines (like diphenhydramine/Benadryl) because it is less likely to cause confusion or sedation. Pregnancy: Talk to your doctor before using loratadine if you are pregnant. It is generally considered low risk, but always check with your healthcare provider. Breastfeeding: Small amounts of loratadine can pass into breast milk. Consult your doctor before using if you are breastfeeding. Kidney or liver disease: You may need a lower dose or less frequent dosing. Talk to your doctor or pharmacist before use. Children under 2 years: Do not give loratadine to children under 2 years of age unless directed by a doctor.
